title: Am I Sikh enough?
hook: cut hair, no amrit, no Punjabi: the Sikh code defines a Sikh by belief, and the gurdwara door is open at every stage

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwara, the door of the Guru: head covered, shoes off, and you're in. Your line was everyone is welcome. Today, the question some people carry to that door and never say out loud. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

A car in a gurdwara parking lot. The engine's off, and nobody gets out. Inside, a young man with short hair is running through a list. My grandfather wore a turban; I don't. I can't read Gurmukhi. I haven't been here since I was a kid. Will people look at me? Am I even allowed to call myself Sikh? A lot of people sit in that car. Some sit there for years. Today, the question, and an honest answer.
screen: `A CAR IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `SHORT HAIR. NO GURMUKHI. YEARS AWAY.` → `AM I SIKH ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Sikh means learner, and a learner, by definition, isn't finished. Then the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct most gurdwaras follow, defines a Sikh first by belief: in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' teaching, and the tenth Guru's amrit, with allegiance to no other religion. It doesn't open with a haircut or a language test. Uncut hair does matter deeply in Sikhi. It's a vow for those who take amrit, and many Sikhs hold that every Sikh should aim to keep it. Sikhs differ, sometimes strongly, on how that applies to someone who isn't there yet. That's a real conversation, and your Keeper is a good person to have it with. What isn't in doubt is the door. Langar feeds whoever sits down. Cover your head, take off your shoes, and you're in. Many Sikhs answer this exact worry with an old saying: the house of Nanak is open to all. And not reading Gurmukhi? Plenty of Sikhs, especially those who grew up far from Punjab, are in exactly that spot, and many learn as adults. So the useful question isn't, am I Sikh enough? It's the learner's question: what's my next step? For one person it's walking in. For another, one bani, or one letter. That's Sikhi: the Sikh way, a path you walk, not a badge you earn before you start.
screen: `SIKH MEANS LEARNER.` · `THE CODE STARTS WITH BELIEF.` · `SIKHS DIFFER ON THE DETAILS.` · `THE DOOR IS OPEN TO ALL.` · then, large: `START WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Picture that parking lot again, and this time it's you in the car, exactly as you are today: your hair, your Punjabi or the lack of it, your questions. Open the door, walk to the shoe rack, slip your shoes off, cover your head, and step inside. Notice any voice that says you're too late, or not enough; let it speak, then let it go quiet. Sit down on the floor beside everyone else, and rest with the breath.
Sikhi. The Sikh way, lived: a path you walk as a learner, starting from wherever you are.
Your line: start where you are. The door was open before you got there. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper.

Replaced 'The flag outside' (word Nishan Sahib). Why: the map's top change is an early, warm answer to 'can I still be Sikh with cut hair / no amrit / no Punjabi?', the most repeated identity question in the Reddit research (REDDIT.md, REDDIT_REPLIES.md §7), which was otherwise answered only at day 272. The Nishan Sahib still lives on day 7 (the Khanda, the flag, the Vaisakhi pole renewal), day 16 (the flag seen from far away) and day 275 (the two Nishan Sahibs at the Akal Takht).

Sensitive (who counts as a Sikh): no ruling is made. The script states the Rehat Maryada's belief-based definition, that kesh matters deeply and is a vow for amritdharis, that many Sikhs hold every Sikh should aim to keep it, and that Sikhs differ on how this applies to non-initiates. It never says anyone is or isn't 'a real Sikh'. Keeper to confirm the tone and the paraphrase of the definition.
'The house of Nanak is open to all' is given as a common saying (it was the top reply in the r/Sikh thread on cut hair); confirm it's fair to call it an old saying.

Language: 'plenty of Sikhs, especially those who grew up far from Punjab' can't read Gurmukhi is kept general on purpose. The map's line that 'most of an estimated 20 million Sikhs' can't speak Punjabi is not used: most Sikhs live in Punjab and speak it.
Day 272 (Many ways of being Sikh) now points back to this day and keeps the deeper teaching (amritdhari, keshdhari, sahajdhari, mona, the court cases).
2026-10-07 (job 2): voice left as rewritten; games.guess added, 'the bell holds the time' cut and the practice's sentences joined (same words otherwise).
